lesson.menu_desc: A settlement meeting with opposing counsel -- how to cut in politely, hold the floor and pick up where you left off -- 33 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 27 -- Objection, Politely
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Rodrigo Marques de França | Lesson 27 -- Objection, Politely
lesson.grammar_point: interrupting, holding and taking back the floor: softened interruptions with could, may and just (could I just come in here, may I just add), holding the floor (if I could just finish, let me just finish this point) and resuming (as I was saying, to get back to my point, where was I)

listenings.text: I study how people take turns in conversation, and the first thing I tell my students is that interrupting is not always rude. In some families, if you wait for a long silence before you speak, you will never speak at all. People overlap, they finish each other's sentences, and nobody is offended. In other places, a two-second pause is a sign of respect, and if you cut in, people think you are not listening. The problem starts when these two styles meet in the same meeting room. The fast talker thinks the quiet one has nothing to say. The quiet one thinks the fast talker is aggressive. So what can you do? First, notice your own style. Secondly, when you need to come in, use a small bridge: 'Sorry, could I just add something here?' It takes two seconds, and it changes everything. And when someone cuts in on you, don't fight. Let them finish, and then say, 'As I was saying...' Nobody will remember the interruption. They will remember that you stayed calm.

I was a trial judge for twenty-two years, and now I work as a mediator, so I have heard a lot of interruptions. In a courtroom, there are rules. If a lawyer thinks a question is unfair, he stands up and says, 'Objection.' The judge decides at once. If I sustain the objection, the witness doesn't answer. If I overrule it, the witness goes on. It is quick and clean, and nobody takes it personally. In a mediation, there are no such rules, and that is where good lawyers show their class. The best ones never raise their voice. When the other side starts to ramble, they wait for a breath and say, 'May I just come in on that point?' When they are interrupted, they say, 'If I could just finish this point, I will hand it straight back to you.' And they always do. My advice is simple. Interrupt the argument, never the person. And when you take the floor back, take it with a smile.
